posts.text:
A country can be free. But are we?

Every Independence Day, we remember the freedom our country fought for.

But I’ve been thinking about a different kind of freedom.

The one that doesn’t need a flag, a parade or a celebration.

The freedom inside our own minds.

Because somewhere along the way, we learn what a “good” career looks like.

What success should look like.

What a successful person should sound like.

What we should want.

And sometimes, without realizing it, we stop asking ourselves:
“Do I actually believe this?”

We start choosing the familiar over the meaningful.

The acceptable over the authentic.

The popular opinion over our own perspective.

And that is where I think freedom of thought becomes important.

Being free doesn’t mean always disagreeing.

It means having the space to question.
To listen without blindly following.
To disagree without disrespect.
To change your mind without shame.
To take a road that may not be the most popular one, but feels right for you.

Because every meaningful shift, whether in society, business or our own lives, begins with someone willing to look at the obvious and ask:
“Could there be another way?”

Maybe that is what we need more of today.

Not louder opinions.
More independent thinking.

Not people trying to be different.
People willing to think deeply enough to form their own point of view.

This Independence Day, I’m celebrating a freedom we often overlook:

The freedom to think.
The freedom to question.
The freedom to choose.
The freedom to become.

Because a free country is a powerful thing.

But a country of free minds can change the world.

Happy Independence Day.

#IndependenceDay #FreedomOfThought #ThoughtLeadership #IndependentThinking #India

Growing up, most of us were told some version of the same thing: don't talk about your achievements, let your work speak for itself...

It's a good value to raise a kid with. 
It's a terrible LinkedIn strategy.

Because here's what's actually happening while you're staying quiet: India is already LinkedIn's second-largest market in the world, with roughly 148 million users, and every one of them is competing for the same recruiter's attention, the same client's inbox, the same 10 seconds of scroll-time.

And the data on what actually wins that attention is pretty stark:

→ People with complete, active LinkedIn profiles are 40 times more likely to be found for opportunities than people with incomplete ones. Not "slightly more visible." 

→ There are now 2.5 applicants for every job posting on LinkedIn, up from just 1.5 in 2022. The bar for getting noticed has gone up, quietly, in just a few years.

→ 74% of people say they trust someone with an established personal brand more than someone without one, and decision-makers now prefer content from individual creators over faceless brand pages more often than not.

→ And this one's the one that gets me: Hinge Research found that professionals with the highest level of visible expertise earn up to 13 times more than equally skilled peers with none. 

Same skill. 
Same years. 
13x the outcome, purely because one person was known and the other wasn't.

None of this is asking you to become someone loud, fake, or "salesy." 
That's not what's working anyway, and it's not who you are.

It's asking you to stop treating visibility like arrogance. They're not the same thing. 

One is bragging. The other is just making sure the people who need what you know can actually find you.

If you've got the skill but not the visibility, that's the easiest gap I know how to close, and usually the one people sit on the longest out of habit, not logic.

Email me at [email protected] or drop a "Hey" in my DMs if you want to talk through what that could look like for you.

I had a conversation recently with someone doing genuinely important work, the kind of research that could change how a whole industry operates in five years, and her LinkedIn had 40 followers and a post from eight months ago.

Not because the work wasn't good. 
Because nobody ever taught her that "the work speaks for itself" isn't actually true. 
Not online, anyway.

This happens constantly with people in science, research, and deep technical fields. 

There's this quiet belief that #credibility comes from the work alone, and that talking about it, plainly, publicly, somehow cheapens it. 

So the posting stops before it starts, and the internet just fills that #silence with people who talk a big game but have far less behind it.

Here's what I've come to believe pretty strongly: being a great scientist and being a known scientist are two completely different skills, and neither one substitutes for the other anymore. 

You can do the most rigorous, careful, quietly brilliant work in your field and still lose funding, visibility, and opportunities to someone doing half the work but all of the talking.

That's not the internet being unfair. 
That's just how attention works now.

The good news is, communicating your work clearly isn't the same as dumbing it down, and it's not some separate personality trait you either have or don't. 

It's a skill, and a learnable one, that most technical people just never got taught alongside their actual expertise.

If that's the gap you've been sitting in, quietly doing excellent work that almost nobody outside your lab or your field actually knows about, email me at [email protected] or drop a "Hey" in my DMs. This is genuinely one of my favorite things to work on.

I keep thinking about something a friend said to me a while back. 

She'd just started posting on LinkedIn and told me, half-joking, "I think I need to sound smarter."

That stuck with me. 
Because that's usually where it goes wrong.

Not because people aren't smart. 
Because the moment you start writing for an audience instead of writing what you actually think, something in the sentence changes. 

It gets careful. Rounder at the edges. Safer. 

And safe is the one thing nobody remembers.

I think what actually happens in those first few weeks of posting isn't a writing problem at all. 

It's that you're meeting a version of yourself you haven't met yet, the one that has opinions in public, and that version feels foreign for a while. Awkward, even. 

You re-read your own sentence and think, did I really say that?

That discomfort isn't a sign to stop. 
It's usually the closest you've gotten to your actual voice all week.

The people who seem to write effortlessly here didn't skip that part. They just stopped showing you the version before the good draft. 

What you're seeing is the fiftieth attempt, not the first.

So if there's a post sitting in your notes app that you've rewritten four times and still haven't published, I'd guess it's not that it's bad. 

I'd guess it's that it finally sounds like you, and that's exactly the kind of uncomfortable that's worth sitting with.

If you want a second pair of eyes on it, or you're just trying to figure out what "sounding like you" actually means on here, email me at [email protected] or drop a "Hey" in my DMs. I like these conversations more than most.

Whenever I look at someone's LinkedIn profile for the first time, there's one thing I check before anything else.

Not the banner. 
Not the headline. 
Not even the About section.

I scroll to their last 5 posts and ask one question: if I removed the name and photo, could I tell this was written by a real, specific person? 

Or could this exact post have been written by literally anyone in their industry?

More often than not, it's the second one.
Not because the person isn't interesting. 
Almost always the opposite, actually. 

It's because somewhere along the way, they started writing what they thought LinkedIn "wanted" instead of what they actually think.

Generic advice. 
Safe opinions. 
The same five hooks everyone's using this month.

Here's the thing though: the algorithm isn't what's punishing that content. 
Boredom is. 

People scroll past "safe" the same way they scroll past an ad.

The profiles that actually build trust, get remembered, and turn into client conversations are the ones where you can feel an actual opinion underneath the polish. A little edge. A real story instead of a case study with the names filed off.

If you read your last 5 posts right now and honestly can't tell they're yours and not a competitor's, that's not a content problem. That's a positioning problem, and it's usually the first thing I look at when I work with someone on their profile.

If that hit a little close to home, email me at [email protected] or just drop a "Hey" in my DMs. Happy to tell you honestly what I see when I look at yours.
